My friend, who followed Apple products with an almost religious zeal — there were many such people in those days — entered the room and announced “This is the convergence!” We spent the next few minutes gaping in awe at the idea that every single piece of portable consumer electronics was about to be combined into a single device. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For many, it felt like a messianic moment. It was a supercomputer in your pocket, a voice for the voiceless, the tricorder </span><em>and </em><span>the communicator from Star Trek, all that and more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was also big money. Years before Benedict Evans wrote “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8ab7cccd-48c5-47ae-aabc-b3daed72b86b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">The smartphone is the new sun</a><span>”, every ambitious tech entrepreneur and content creator in America was in on the game. Social media — that infinitely scrolling vertical feed — was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b5f7e619-8061-4c5b-8eac-5448aab69922?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the killer app of the smartphone</a><span>, what the spreadsheet had been for the PC or e-commerce had been for the internet. In 2012, Facebook’s monster IPO kicked off a gold rush, and everyone moved to San Francisco to strike it rich. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But you didn’t need to be a tech entrepreneur in order to get in on the action. The smartphone meant far more eyeballs glued to far more screens for far more minutes of the day, and that meant dollar signs for content creators. YouTubers, Instagram fashion influencers, and Twitter activists became whole new economic classes. Old-style content businesses like newspapers and TV networks saw their doom, but also a potential lifeline. (Eventually even econ bloggers got our piece of the pie; plenty of you signed up for this blog through a scrollable app.)</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Beautiful design coupled with brilliant engineering. Technology anyone could use. Economic opportunity for the masses </span><em>and </em><span>for the elite. A way to have your ideas and opinions heard by millions of people thousands of miles away, at any hour of any day. No wonder Steve Jobs was the last technologist that everyone agreed was an American hero. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But when I recall that fateful day in 2007, I remember not joy, but a sudden surge of foreboding. That was strange, and out of character for me. I’ve always been a technophile at heart — I grew up as a hardcore Star Trek fan, and until that moment in 2007, each new marvel — broadband, the internet, the laptop computer, etc. — had felt like it was moving us toward that bold utopian future. The iPhone felt different. Some small voice in the back of my head told me: “This is a mistake.” And though I tried to ignore that voice for many years, it remained.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What was I worried about? The printing press, the car and the telephone had offered freedom from the crushing conformity of small-town life. When broadcast television threatened to smother us with a centrally dictated monoculture, it sparked a decades-long resistance. When the internet arrived, we spent two decades using it to revel in our individuality — we made our personal websites, started blogs, joined small online communities centered around our interests. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Sometime around 2014 or 2015 we woke up to the fact that the world of the Old Internet no longer existed. “The internet” no longer meant the Web — it meant a tiny handful of big platforms. Twitter and Reddit for screaming about politics, Facebook and Instagram for being jealous of your friends’ vacation pics. Gone were the days of painting our individuality on the canvas of the Web. The platforms were the hive minds, we were the neurons, and the smartphone was the axon that kept each of us wired tight into the collective.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“‘Social media is bad,’ he typed on social media!!” This is the perpetual and instantaneous response of many of the neurons…er, people…in my timeline. Indeed, if social media is so bad, why don’t you just put down the phone? But this idea displays a fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of network effects. Suppose I decide to get off Instagram and go play pickup basketball instead. If everyone </span><em>else </em><span>is on Instagram instead of playing pickup basketball, who am I going to play with?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is an extreme and simplified example, obviously, but the intuition here comes from real research. FOMO is not utility; it’s a bad equilibrium. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s also an impulse to do a sort of “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d2e7702-710c-43c5-931e-c1435efe2665?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Good Tsar, bad boyars</a><span>” maneuver, where people say “it’s not the phones, it’s social media”. This intervention </span><strong>specifically targeted the feature that makes smartphones "smart" (mobile internet)</strong><span> while allowing participants to maintain mobile connection (through texts and calls) and </span><strong>nonmobile access to the internet</strong><span> (e.g. through desktop computers). The intervention improved mental health, subjective well-being, and objectively measured ability to sustain attention; 91% of participants improved on at least one of these outcomes. Mediation analyses suggest that these improvements can be partially explained by the intervention's impact on how people spent their time; when people did not have access to mobile internet, they </span><strong>spent more time socializing in person</strong><span>, exercising, and being in nature. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Other recent experiments have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d42c85e9-930f-4fc2-b1b6-cfc7e035ba69?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">yielded similar results</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The likeliest explanation is that there is simply something thin and insufficient about online interaction. It’s lacking in some essential emotional nutrient that human beings evolved to harvest from the physical proximity of other human beings. Perhaps it’s something cognitive — the richness of context that tells you that no, your friend’s life isn’t perfect just because they posted a cool video of their trip to Europe, and thus you don’t need to feel constantly envious and inadequate and left-out. Or perhaps it’s something physical — the tiny touch of a high-five or a hug, the simple feeling of the proximity of other human bodies. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Whatever this emotional nutrient is, our young people are starving for it, while they binge on the cheap sugar-alcohol of emoji reactions and story views. In other parts of the world, young people are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0008a2af-7e22-49e2-a00c-c9ba8990c695?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">just starting to break free of this collective trap</a><span>, but not yet in the United States.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But making teenagers sad is one thing; putting an end to the Human Age on planet Earth is quite another.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The global fertility decline is a long-standing trend. Every country that escapes poverty, urbanizes, and teaches its people to read is going to transition from a high fertility rate (5-7 children per woman) to a much lower rate. Long before the smartphone burst on the scene, most of Europe and the richer parts of East Asia had fallen below replacement-level fertility. Everyone would crack jokes about Japan not having enough kids. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then the 2010s came, and then the 2020s, and suddenly it wasn’t just Japan. In fact, Japan now has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b2c3a45-eb4e-400c-9a1e-76c9b46585d2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">one of the higher fertility rates in East Asia</a><span>, at a still-catastrophic 1.15. Thailand’s fertility has reached 0.78, South Korea’s is back up to 0.92 after record levels of economic incentives for childbearing, China’s is down to 0.90 and falling. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The rest of the world isn’t far behind. India is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/276b2bc9-3c80-4227-ae75-99dc819e88a1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">below replacement</a><span>. Latin America is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0d6138a1-01a0-4b0b-9803-e84750d687cb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">starting to look like Europe</a><span>. Mexico’s fertility is below America’s. The United States, which had long resisted the low-fertility trend among rich countries, just hit a record low of 1.57. Islam is no defense; the Middle East’s fertility is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c569c67e-1df3-4489-b12a-460dc7d49caa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">cratering</a><span>. The only region with high birth rates now is Africa, whose fertility rate has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aac8fbe5-71bb-4379-8081-8047092c7c90?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">fallen from over 7 to under 4</a><span>, and is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e9794229-30be-4247-a0f4-80a7d26bb993?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">falling much faster than anyone expected</a><span>. The world itself </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a30ae55-167d-4adf-98e6-3c09a6cd2537?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">may already be below replacement</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why is fertility falling everywhere across the globe, to such low levels, all at once? Whatever the cause is, it can’t be something local and parochial. It can’t be the effect of America’s Great Recession, or Confucian culture, or whatever. It has to be something that has been affecting </span><em>the entire world at the same time</em><span>, and that narrows it down to a pretty short list. And the biggest global technological change of the 2010s was the introduction of the smartphone.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s not hard to come up with a plausible theory of why smartphones might cause people to stop having children — in fact, it’s a lot easier to explain than teen unhappiness. Childbearing requires physical contact; the kind of digital interaction provided by smartphones cannot provide that contact. So when human interaction shifts to the digital realm, whether it’s social media, dating apps, chat groups, or online pornography, </span><em>fewer children result</em><span>, simply because there are fewer chances for the type of physical interaction that creates children.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And now it’s time for data. There are no actual experiments here; no one has gone around giving out iPhones to see if the recipients end up having fewer children. But we can occasionally find differences in the speed at which smartphones arrived in various places, and we can look at how that affected fertility. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s what Caitlyn Myers and Ezekiel Hooper do in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f4fac39e-fbb9-4cb3-ab49-ed581b9f46d7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">their new paper</a><span> “Is the iPhone Birth Control? Causal Evidence from AT&T’s 2007–2011 Carrier Monopoly”. They write:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The U.S. general fertility rate has fallen by 22% since 2007, a sustained decline not readily explained by economic conditions, contraceptive use, housing or childcare costs, or other commonly cited factors. We assess the potential role of a different shock: the diffusion of the smartphone. The U.S. rollout of the iPhone, the first modern smartphone, provides a natural experiment: from June 2007 through February 2011, the device was sold only on AT&T, allowing us to identify its effect from variation in AT&T’s mobile broadband coverage…[A]ccess to the iPhone reduced births by 4.5–8.0% at ages 15–19 and 3.2–6.6% at ages 20–24…Overall, the diffusion of the iPhone explains 33–52% of the decline in the general fertility rate among women aged 15–44. National-survey evidence on time use and sexual behavior is consistent with the iPhone reducing in-person interactions, increasing pornography use, and reducing sexual frequency.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Myers and Hooper are not the only ones to find this result. Hudson and Boedo (2026) find that teen fertility collapsed in the U.S., England, and Wales when teens shifted from physical to online interaction:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Teen fertility collapsed globally starting around 2007. This affected countries across the income and policy spectrum. This paper argues that smartphones changed how teens spend time with each other, and that this change in turn drove the collapse in teen fertility. Sitting at home wouldn’t be appealing without the digital technologies!</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If Stone’s idea of a “new selfishness” is right, it hints at something more going on than just “fewer opportunities for young people to have sex”. Among all the reasons humans bore children — labor for the farm, income support in old age, religious norms, sheer accident, and so on — one of the most powerful reasons was probably to </span><em>grow your own community. </em><span>Humans need human company, and throughout most of history, the surest way to get more company was to create it yourself. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Urbanization disrupts the need to grow your own community, by giving you a community of strangers. Fertility rates have always been much lower in cities than in the countryside, and when countries become more urbanized and wealthy, their birth rates drop. But urban friends move away, or withdraw to the suburbs to have their own kids, or outgrow the friend group. The digital companions in your smartphone screen, however — the strangers who argue with you on X, the acquaintances who post their stories on Insta, the imaginary friends of TikTok, the faux lovers of OnlyFans — never desert you. Smartphones permanently short-circuit the deep-seated human need to have your kids keep you company. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So…it’s the phones.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I suspect that a lot of people simply don’t </span><em>want</em><span> it to be the phones. We want the Spirit of 2007 back. We want technology to feel unambiguously </span><em>good</em><span> again. We want to believe in Saint Steve Jobs, the last of the American techno-heroes. We among the commentariat want to believe that the innovation that has given us our social status and our high incomes was not also something that — if its effect goes unchecked — will end the human age on planet Earth. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the data can’t be denied, we will begin to tell ourselves that it’s actually a </span><em>good </em><span>thing. Teen pregnancy is bad, right? (Let’s ignore the fact that the research shows smartphones suppressing fertility among older cohorts.) What’s wrong with fewer humans, anyway? We could all use a little elbow room, right? And won’t AI take all the jobs anyway? </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is what humanity’s remaining young people call “cope”. The end of the Anthropocene — and that’s what it means, if fertility declines are driven by the presence of technology that never goes away — is unlikely to be easy or pretty. If AI doesn’t take all the jobs, then </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b8952817-c6bc-421c-9894-b966fd21a7c4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a shrinking humanity means a world of toil</a><span> for the young people who remain. If AI </span><em>does</em><span> take the jobs, then that toil will be averted, but humanity’s end will be correspondingly weirder. Here is what I wrote last year:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Thus, dimly and through the fog, we can begin to perceive the shape of the future that the posthuman age will take. As humanity becomes more tightly bound into a single digital collective, we find that we desire offline families less and less. As we gradually abandon reproduction, there are fewer and fewer of us, forcing us to cling even more tightly to the online collective — to spend more of our time online, to take solace in the ever-denser core of the final global village. The god-mind of that collective delivers us riches undreamt of by our ancestors, but we enjoy that bounty in solitude as we wirehead into the hive mind for a bit of company.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Go outside and look up at the night sky. The stars above you are quiet. We have received no transmissions, seen no great works of stellar engineering, met no pointy-eared friends from afar. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/49cec5b3-afa9-43f1-83d5-d1c7cf961c47?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">There seems to be a Great Filter</a><span> that has scoured the Universe of intelligent life as we know it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s possible that we have now found that filter. Perhaps it’s not nukes, or bioweapons, or self-improving AI, or the intransigence of interstellar distances. Perhaps it’s simply the fact that </span><em>biological evolution does not prepare any sentient species for technological evolution</em><span>. When innovation begins, biological beings and their societies adapt and survive for a while, but as technological change accelerates, it inevitably overwhelms hardwired biology’s speed of adaptation. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The destroyer of our species won’t necessarily come in a rain of fire, an apocalyptic plague, or an armada of drones descending on us from the sky. It may be something we excitedly pay $1000 for every three or four years. All that’s required for our species to go from the masters of the Earth to a memory in the circuits of Claude is that we decide to forsake each other’s company to stare eternally into a black
